mappings.note: Greek satraps turning into independent Indo-Greek kings. Political narrative of a dynasty's origin, so the goal rather than an administrative measure.
Asks for an instance of cultural blending - the Heliodorus pillar, Indian deities on Indo-Greek coins. Cultural history read from sources.
The Shaka Samvat and its 78-year offset from the Gregorian calendar. Chronology, which no LO covers.
Describes the reach of the Kushana empire from Central Asia into north India. Historical geography; the item on why route control mattered carries LO-101 instead.

'Maharaja rajadhiraja devaputra' read as lofty claims to imperial and divine authority - the self-presentation of a ruler's power. Not CG-SST2, because the titles are analysed as instruments of authority.

Kanishka's coins showing Buddha and Shiva read as patronage of several faiths - a ruler's policy towards religious communities, the same treatment as the Satavahana and Kharavela patronage items. Not LO-104, because no movement's emergence is analysed.
Control of the Silk Route letting the Kushanas tax trade and build influence is a strategy for holding and exploiting territory. Not CG-SST2, since the question is why control mattered to the state.
The key difference between the two sculpture schools in material, style and region. Art history under the goal; LO-103 covers buildings.
The range of Indian deities and nature spirits shown by the Mathura school. Iconography, so the goal rather than the architecture outcome.

Traces how Kushana-period religious imagery prepared the way for later temple architecture - explicitly a development leading to temples, which is LO-103's subject. Not CG-SST2, because the question is about architectural development.
The epics reaching near-final form in this period. Literary and textual history under the goal.

A goldsmith's inscription on a stone yaksha read as evidence that artisans worked across crafts - social and economic inference from an inscription. Not LO-103, since no building technique is involved.

A widowed Satavahana queen performing the ashvamedha and making grants, read as real religious and political authority. Authority and ritual claim to power, so LO-101; the naming-tradition items stay with the goal as social history.
Holding contested borders to keep the core territory safe is a strategy of military control. Not CG-SST2, because the reasoning is about defence.

Roman pottery, ship coins, warehouses and a guild's donation inscription all have to be read as evidence of a trading post and its patronage. Archaeological inference throughout, which is the goal's own clause.

Parts (i) and (ii) are about the Mathura and Gandhara schools (CG-SST2), while part (iii) asks what a governor gained politically by commissioning blended art (LO-101). Not LO-103, because the commission concerns sculpture rather than building technique.
Choosing the ashvamedha to claim supremacy without immediate war, and the risk that it invites battle, is statecraft weighed against military cost. The clearest LO-101 reading of the rite.
Reads Sangam poems on Puhar for trade and taxation and then asks how reliable poetry is as economic evidence. Part (iii) is a question about historical method, squarely the goal.
Weighs inscriptions and coins as historical sources for the period. The most explicit 'how historians study the past' item in the chapter.

Evaluates women's roles from queens' inscriptions and reports of women fighters, and warns against generalising from thin evidence. Social history plus source criticism; the civics outcome on women's disadvantages concerns the present day.

Compares why two empires fell - weak central control, breakaway regions, fiscal strain. Reasoning about the limits of imperial control, so LO-101; LO-102 would require the rulers' policies rather than their collapses to be set against each other.
The Kannagi story used to draw out a king's dharma of delivering swift and accurate justice - the norms of rule. Not CG-SST2, because the epic is the vehicle and royal duty is what is examined.
'Devaputra' analysed as a claim to divine mandate legitimising rule over diverse subjects. Imperial authority, so LO-101 rather than the religion outcome.
Warfare and matrimonial diplomacy weighed as alternative routes to power. Both are strategies of control, which LO-101 names. Not LO-102, because no two named rulers are compared.
Argues that regional powers and cultural identities of this age prepared the ground for later empires. A long-run historical judgement under the goal.
The fullest account of why the period is called an age of reorganisation - fragmentation, new kingdoms, invasions, cultural change. Period characterisation.

Sets Pushyamitra's Vedic ashvamedha against Kharavela's Jain devotion and claimed benevolence - a direct comparison of two rulers' strategies for legitimacy. Exactly LO-102, where the single-ruler items take LO-101.
Satavahana indigenous culture set beside Roman trade links, argued from coins and finds. Cultural and economic history under the goal.
The Sangam Age's significance for South Indian literature, society and identity. Cultural history and source value, so the goal.

Analyses assimilation under Indo-Greek and Kushana rule - adopted religions, fused art, naturalised names. A cultural-development item; LO-104 would need a new movement to be emerging rather than existing faiths adopted.
The development and traits of the two art schools and what their coexistence says about cultural dynamics. Sculpture and cultural history, not building technique, so not LO-103.

The economic half - taxing Silk Route trade for revenue - is LO-101, while the cultural half, including Buddhism travelling to Central Asia and China, is a broad historical development under CG-SST2. The question asks for both.

The spear signals royal and military authority and the Buddha image signals patronage (LO-101), while part (iii) asks what Greek lettering on an Indian coin reveals about the empire's reach and mixed culture (CG-SST2).
